title: National Cable & Telecommunications Association v. Brand X Internet Services (2005)
shortTitle: National Cable & Telecommunications Association v. Brand X Internet Services (2005)
summary: A court's earlier reading of an ambiguous statute does not bind an agency under Chevron unless the court held that the statute was unambiguous.
notes:
Key line: "A court's prior judicial construction of a statute trumps an agency construction otherwise entitled to Chevron deference only if the prior court decision holds that its construction follows from the unambiguous terms of the statute and thus leaves no room for agency discretion." Justice Thomas, for the Court.

Citation: 545 U.S. 967 (2005).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were the National Cable & Telecommunications Association, a cable industry trade group, and the Federal Communications Commission together with the United States. Respondents were Brand X Internet Services, an independent internet service provider, along with other ISPs, consumer groups and state regulators who had challenged the FCC's order. The ISPs wanted access to cable companies' transmission lines on common-carrier terms. The cable companies and the FCC defended the order that classified cable broadband as an information service and kept it free of mandatory common-carrier regulation under Title II of the Communications Act.
sections.Material Facts: The Communications Act, as amended in 1996, subjects providers of telecommunications service to common-carrier duties but not providers of information service. A telecommunications service is the offering of telecommunications for a fee directly to the public. In March 2002 the FCC issued a Declaratory Ruling concluding that cable modem service is an information service and not also a telecommunications service, because the consumer uses the high-speed wire to receive an integrated offering of internet access, and the transmission component is not offered separately. Two years earlier, in AT&T Corp. v. City of Portland (2000), the Ninth Circuit had held that cable modem service was part telecommunications service and part information service, in a case that involved no FCC interpretation.
sections.Procedural History: Numerous parties petitioned for review of the Declaratory Ruling, and the petitions were consolidated in the Ninth Circuit. That court vacated the ruling in part. It held that its own prior construction in Portland controlled under stare decisis and that the Chevron framework therefore did not apply, so the FCC could not classify cable modem service as solely an information service. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to the cable association and to the FCC and reversed on June 27, 2005, remanding for further proceedings.
sections.Issue: The FCC classified cable modem service as an information service, freeing cable companies from common-carrier duties, after the Ninth Circuit had already read the statute differently in a case decided without any agency interpretation before it. The Ninth Circuit then treated its own precedent as controlling. Was the FCC's classification of cable modem service as an information service, and not a telecommunications service, a lawful construction of the Communications Act under Chevron and the APA, and does a court's prior construction of an ambiguous statute foreclose an agency from adopting a different reasonable reading?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Ninth Circuit erred in treating its prior construction as controlling; a judicial precedent forecloses an agency reading only when the court held the statute unambiguous. The word offering in the definition of telecommunications service is ambiguous as applied to cable modem service, and the FCC's conclusion that cable companies do not offer a stand-alone transmission service is reasonable. The classification was also not arbitrary and capricious despite the different treatment of DSL. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Thomas applied Chevron in two steps. Under Chevron, ambiguity in a statute the agency administers is a delegation to the agency, so a court's own earlier reading fills the gap only provisionally. If the earlier decision rested on the best reading rather than the only permissible reading, the agency remains free to adopt a different reasonable construction, and the court must accept it. Portland had not held the statute unambiguous, so the FCC was not bound. On the merits, the Court found the statute ambiguous. Whether a cable company offers telecommunications depends on whether the transmission is a stand-alone offering or an integrated part of a finished product, as when a car dealer sells a car and does not separately offer the engine. The FCC reasonably concluded that consumers buy internet access as a whole, using transmission to reach functions like email and web browsing. The Court rejected the argument that the FCC's earlier treatment of DSL as telecommunications service made the ruling arbitrary; the agency explained that it was reconsidering DSL and that the two markets developed differently. The Court also declined to find that the Computer II precedents required a different result, because those rules addressed telephone companies with existing common-carrier obligations.

topics.lrs-i-historical-chevron: Brand X extended Chevron’s allocation of interpretive choice to conflicts with some earlier judicial constructions.
topics.lrs-i-statutory-stare-decisis: The later note uses Brand X to question the precise content of Chevron-era holdings after Loper Bright.
topics.lrs-i-independent-judgment: Loper Bright's rejection of ambiguity-based deference undercuts Brand X's rule that agencies can displace prior judicial constructions.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Justice Stevens concurred, noting that the rule about prior judicial constructions would not apply to a Supreme Court decision. Justice Breyer concurred, agreeing that Chevron applied even though the FCC acted by declaratory ruling. Justice Scalia dissented, joined by Justices Souter and Ginsburg as to Part I, arguing that cable companies plainly offer telecommunications to the public and that the majority's rule lets agencies override judicial precedent, which he called bizarre.
